summary:
SPACEMIRROR is a comparative planetary analog study and interactive spatial mapping project designed to identify Earth locations that replicate the environmental conditions of permanent Moon bases and Mars missions. By integrating open datasets from NASA (PDS, LRO, MRO, Earthdata) and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA RADARSAT), we evaluated terrestrial sites across five quantitative parameters: geology, terrain, climate, radiation, and subsurface dynamics.

Our analysis systematically paired and scored five optimal terrestrial analogs against critical extraterrestrial targets—including Don Juan Pond (Hale Crater, 89.0%), Mount Suswa (Marius Hills, 85.1%), Kamil Crater (Linné Crater, 82.4%), Dallol Springs (Gusev Crater, 79.3%), and Tenoumer Crater (Victoria Crater, 76.8%)—visualized through an interactive geographic map and a structured evaluation matrix.

Testing space hardware and habitats directly in deep space carries immense financial and operational risks. SPACEMIRROR bridges this gap by pinpointing accessible, scientifically validated Earth proving grounds for cryogenic drilling, subsurface lava-tube habitat deployment, rover traction testing, and hardware durability validation—accelerating mission readiness while significantly reducing pre-launch costs.

1. Functionality and Methodology (How It Works) SPACEMIRROR is a comparative planetary analog analysis framework and interactive geographic mapping project designed to identify terrestrial environments that replicate the physical, geological, and climatic conditions of permanent Moon base candidates and Mars exploration targets. Rather than relying on single-variable comparisons, our methodology cross-references remote sensing datasets from NASA (PDS, LRO, MRO, Earthdata) and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA RADARSAT) across five quantitative evaluation criteria: geology, terrain morphology, climate, radiation shielding, and subsurface dynamics. Each terrestrial site is systematically paired with an extraterrestrial target and assigned a composite similarity score—such as Don Juan Pond to Hale Crater (89.0%), Mount Suswa to Marius Hills (85.1%), Kamil Crater to Linné Crater (82.4%), Dallol Springs to Gusev Crater (79.3%), and Tenoumer Crater to Victoria Crater (76.8%).

2. Benefits and Intended Impact Conducting hardware, habitat, and rover testing directly in deep space entails extreme financial costs and mission-critical risks. SPACEMIRROR provides mission planners, researchers, and aerospace engineers with accessible, scientifically validated Earth proving grounds. By highlighting both shared characteristics and quantitative divergences (such as atmospheric pressure or gravity differences), the project allows teams to accurately calibrate cryogenic drilling tools, test inflatable subsurface habitats inside lava tubes, evaluate rover wheel traction on sharp regolith analogs, and validate hardware durability against extreme acidity and aeolian dust. This accelerates pre-launch readiness while reducing mission development expenditures.

3. Tools, Software, and Technologies Used

  • Scientific Data & Remote Sensing Archives: NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO LOLA/LROC/Diviner), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO HiRISE/CRISM), NASA Earthdata (ASTER/SRTM), and CSA RADARSAT-1 / RCM datasets.
  • Development & Visualization: HTML5, CSS3, and custom inline SVG graphics for structured visual presentation and data matrices, paired with an interactive spatial web map accessible via QR integration.
  • AI & Analytical Assistance: Generative AI (Large Language Models) was utilized strictly to assist in structuring analytical matrices, formatting HTML/CSS presentation layouts, and refining academic English documentation.

4. Creativity and Key Factors Considered Unlike traditional analog studies that focus solely on geological composition, SPACEMIRROR introduces a balanced multi-criteria weighting system alongside explicit "Quantitative Divergence" metrics. Acknowledging that no Earth site is a 100% mirror of another world, our team explicitly accounted for terrestrial variables—such as higher Earth gravity (9.81 m/s29.81 m/s2 vs. Mars 3.72 m/s23.72 m/s2), atmospheric pressure differentials, and terrestrial biosphere interference—so engineers understand the exact physical limitations of each test site before conducting field simulations.
